questions.question: During the day, your headlight should:

options.text: Not be used.
Be used on high beam.
Be used on low beam.
Switch between high beam and low beam.

questions.explanation: Using high beam headlights during the day helps other drivers see you. Use high beam any time you are not riding behind or approaching another vehicle.

questions.question: When riding in a group, inexperienced riders should position themselves:

options.text: Just behind the leader.
In front of the group.
At the rear of the group.
Beside the leader.

questions.explanation: Inexperienced riders should ride just behind the leader. This position lets experienced riders behind them watch and help if needed.

questions.question: How does stopping distance for motorcycles compare to stopping distance for cars?

options.text: Cars need much longer to stop.
Cars need a little longer to stop.
Motorcycles need longer to stop.
Both take about the same amount of time to stop.

questions.correctAnswerText: Both take about the same amount of time to stop.
questions.explanation: Under normal conditions, motorcycles and cars have nearly the same stopping distance. Wet pavement makes it harder for motorcycles to stop quickly.

questions.question: When going through a curve, you should:

options.text: Always stay in the same part of the lane throughout the curve.
Always stay in the left part of the lane throughout the curve.
Always stay in the right part of the lane throughout the curve.
Remember that the best path may not follow the curve of the road.

questions.correctAnswerText: Remember that the best path may not follow the curve of the road.
questions.explanation: Road and traffic conditions change all the time. Be ready to change your lane position as needed. The best path through a curve may not follow the curve of the road exactly.

questions.question: Your lane position should do all of the following, except:

options.text: Increase your ability to see and be seen.
Avoid other drivers' blind spots.
Avoid surface hazards.
Block access to an escape route.

questions.correctAnswerText: Block access to an escape route.
questions.explanation: Good lane position helps you see others and be seen. It helps you avoid wind blasts, blind spots, and surface hazards. Your lane position should also give you an escape route if a hazard appears.

questions.question: The center portion of a lane often contains an oily strip. This strip:

options.text: Is not safe for motorcyclists at any time.
Is usually safe for motorcyclists, unless it is raining.
Should always be avoided since other parts of the lane do not have the oily strip.
Adds to traction for most motorcycle tires.

questions.correctAnswerText: Is usually safe for motorcyclists, unless it is raining.
questions.explanation: Oil drippings from cars collect in the center of a traffic lane. When the road is dry, this area usually has enough traction for motorcycles. The oily strip is usually narrow enough that you can ride to one side and still stay in the center portion of the lane.

questions.question: When being passed, do not move to the far side of your lane because:

options.text: The passing vehicle may re-enter your lane too early.
You may block another vehicle from passing you.
The side of the lane nearest the passing vehicle is better.
You are more likely to feel a wind blast from the passing vehicle.

questions.correctAnswerText: The passing vehicle may re-enter your lane too early.
questions.explanation: When being passed, do not ride on the far side of your lane. This may encourage the passing driver to return to your lane before it is safe to do so.

questions.question: If it starts to rain while you are riding, it is a good idea to:

options.text: Ride down the center of the lane.
Increase your speed.
Ride in the tire tracks left by cars.
Pull onto the shoulder of the road.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride in the tire tracks left by cars.
questions.explanation: The center strip of a lane is hazardous when wet due to oil deposits. When rain starts, ride in the tire tracks left by cars. Slow down on wet surfaces.

questions.question: A helmeted rider is _______ more likely to survive a crash than a rider without a helmet.

options.text: Two times
Three times
Six times
20 times

questions.explanation: Riders who wear helmets are three times more likely to survive a crash than riders who do not wear helmets.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a possible cause of a wobble on your motorcycle?

options.text: Incorrect tire pressure
Improper loading
Unsuitable accessories
Uneven road

questions.explanation: Most wobbles are caused by improper loading, unsuitable accessories, or incorrect tire pressure. Do not accelerate to get out of a wobble.

questions.question: How do you get maximum braking power?

options.text: Use the rear brake only.
Use the front brake only.
Use both brakes.
Use the rear brake and downshift.

questions.explanation: Use both the front and rear brakes together to stop in a straight line. Do not lock either wheel. Always use both brakes when you slow down or stop.

questions.question: What does swerving a motorcycle require?

options.text: A lot of traction.
Little traction.
It is a slow maneuver.
You should do it to avoid a hazard on a slippery road.

questions.explanation: Swerving is a quick move that needs a lot of traction to do safely. Do not swerve on slippery surfaces because sudden moves are dangerous when traction is low.

questions.question: When looking through a turn, what should you turn?

options.text: Just your head.
Your head and shoulders.
Just your shoulders.
Your entire body.

questions.explanation: Look through the turn to see where you want to go. Turn only your head, not your shoulders. Keep your eyes level with the horizon.

questions.question: If your front tire locks while braking, what should you do?

options.text: Keep the brake engaged until you stop.
Release both brakes and coast to a stop.
Release the front brake and use only the rear brake.
Release the brake lever until the tire grips again.

questions.correctAnswerText: Release the brake lever until the tire grips again.
questions.explanation: If your front wheel locks during braking, release the brake lever so the tire can grip the road again. Then apply the brake once more.

questions.question: How do you swerve correctly?

options.text: Shift your weight quickly.
Turn the handlebars quickly.
Press the handgrip in the direction you want to turn.
Press the handgrip in the opposite direction of the turn.

questions.correctAnswerText: Press the handgrip in the direction you want to turn.
questions.explanation: To swerve, press the handgrip on the side you want to turn. Press the opposite handgrip to return to your original direction after you pass the hazard.

questions.question: When stopping behind another vehicle, what should you do?

options.text: Stop far back, then slowly creep forward.
Stay well behind the vehicle.
Make a quick stop right behind it.
Stay about four car lengths back.

questions.explanation: Keep a safe distance behind the vehicle in front of you, even when stopped. The vehicle may back up unexpectedly. You also need space to move if another vehicle comes toward you from behind.

questions.question: When entering a turn, what should a rider do?

options.text: Speed up.
Slow down.
Lean shoulders to match the turn angle.
Sit as high as possible.

questions.explanation: Before entering a turn, slow down by releasing the throttle and using both brakes if needed.

questions.question: Why should you not ride too far right on a three-wheeled motorcycle or with a sidecar?

options.text: Other drivers may not see you.
You will not pass other vehicles as easily.
Other drivers may try to share your lane.
You may run off the road.

questions.correctAnswerText: You may run off the road.
questions.explanation: A sidecar extends to the right side of a motorcycle. Riding too far to the right risks the sidecar leaving the road. On a three-wheeled motorcycle, the right rear wheel may leave the road if you get too close to the right edge.

questions.question: What is the best formation for a group of riders entering a curve?

options.text: Pyramid
Staggered
Single-file
Compressed

questions.explanation: A staggered formation works well for a group on straight roads and allows each rider space to stay safe. Use a single-file formation when turning, entering or leaving a highway, or on curves.

questions.question: On a slippery surface, which should you NOT do?

options.text: Reduce your speed.
Avoid making sudden moves.
Use only the front brake when slowing or stopping.
Use both brakes when slowing or stopping.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use only the front brake when slowing or stopping.
questions.explanation: On slippery surfaces, use both brakes when slowing or stopping, reduce your speed, and avoid sudden moves. Watch for oily areas, dirt, gravel, shaded spots, and bridges—these are more likely to be slippery.

questions.question: When riding a three-wheeled motorcycle through a curve, what should you do?

options.text: Stay in the center of the lane.
Stay on the outside of the lane.
Change your path as needed.
Use the shoulder.

questions.explanation: Three-wheeled motorcycles turn differently than two-wheeled motorcycles. The best path through a curve may not follow the curve exactly. You may need to move from the outside of the curve to the inside before straightening out.

questions.question: When is it important to flash your brake light?

options.text: When approaching a police officer.
When someone is following too closely.
When there is a stop sign ahead.
When your signals are not working.

questions.correctAnswerText: When someone is following too closely.
questions.explanation: Flash your brake light before you slow down if another driver is following too closely. The other driver may not notice the hazard ahead that is making you slow down. Also flash your brake light when you slow down unexpectedly.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of riding in a close group?

options.text: It takes up minimal space on the highway.
The group is easy to see.
The group is unlikely to be split up.
Riders will reach their destination faster in a close group than in a spread out group.

questions.correctAnswerText: Riders will reach their destination faster in a close group than in a spread out group.
questions.explanation: Riding in a close group is better because it uses less road space, is easier for other drivers to see, and is less likely to get separated at traffic lights and during passes. Traveling speed is not affected.

questions.question: What does this hand signal mean?

options.text: Plans to turn left.
Is about to stop.
Plans to turn right.
Is about to slow down.

questions.explanation: Hand signals are used instead of turn signals. If the left arm is bent at the elbow and pointing upward, it means the rider plans to turn right or change lanes to the right.

questions.question: Why should you not change gears on railroad tracks?

options.text: Your motorcycle may stall.
You might go too fast.
Other drivers may not be expecting you to change gears.
The uneven surface may make it difficult to switch gears.

questions.explanation: Do not shift gears when crossing railroad tracks. Your motorcycle might stall while on the tracks.
